```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 0.3, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
ans_col <- rgb(200, 0, 130, maxColorValue = 255)

# fill-in table drawn as a plot; fill_cols are drawn in the answer color, italic
blank_table <- function(headers, body, col_widths = NULL,
                        header_height = 0.35, row_height = 0.5,
                        cex = 0.95, family = "serif", fill_cols = integer(0)) {
  nc <- length(headers); nr <- length(body)
  if (is.null(col_widths)) col_widths <- rep(1, nc)
  col_widths <- col_widths / sum(col_widths)
  cx <- c(0, cumsum(col_widths))
  h_total <- header_height + nr * row_height
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0), family = family)
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, h_total), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  y <- h_total
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  y <- y - header_height
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    y <- y - row_height
    segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = if (i == nr) 1.5 else 0.5,
             col = if (i == nr) "black" else "grey70")
  }
  for (v in cx) segments(v, 0, v, h_total, lwd = 1)
  yh <- h_total - header_height / 2
  for (j in seq_len(nc)) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yh, labels = headers[[j]], font = 2, cex = cex)
  y <- h_total - header_height
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    yc <- y - row_height / 2
    for (j in seq_len(nc)) {
      val <- body[[i]][[j]]
      ans <- j %in% fill_cols && !identical(val, "(none)")
      if (!identical(val, "")) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yc, labels = val, cex = cex,
                                    col = if (ans) ans_col else "black", font = if (ans) 3 else 1)
    }
    y <- y - row_height
  }
}

library(mvtnorm)
library(glmmTMB)
snow <- read.csv("../../data/SnowCourses.csv")
snow$elev_km <- (snow$elev_m - 2400) / 1000
fit_lm <- lm(swe_cm ~ elev_km, data = snow)
X <- model.matrix(fit_lm)
y <- snow$swe_cm
D <- as.matrix(dist(snow[, c("x_km", "y_km")]))
nll_spatial <- function(par) {
  V <- exp(par[3])^2 * exp(-D / exp(par[4])) + exp(par[5])^2 * diag(length(y))
  -dmvnorm(y, as.vector(X %*% par[1:2]), V, log = TRUE)
}
check_val <- nll_spatial(c(40, 40, log(8), log(10), log(3)))
fit <- optim(c(40, 40, log(8), log(10), log(3)), nll_spatial, method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE)
stopifnot(fit$convergence == 0)
beta <- fit$par[1:2]
se <- sqrt(diag(solve(fit$hessian)))
sigma_s <- exp(fit$par[3])
ell <- exp(fit$par[4])
sigma_e <- exp(fit$par[5])
V <- sigma_s^2 * exp(-D / ell) + sigma_e^2 * diag(length(y))

# prediction at a site: regression part, kriging prediction, weights
krige <- function(x0, y0, elev_m) {
  d0 <- sqrt((snow$x_km - x0)^2 + (snow$y_km - y0)^2)
  k0 <- sigma_s^2 * exp(-d0 / ell)
  w <- solve(V, k0)
  reg <- beta[1] + beta[2] * (elev_m - 2400) / 1000
  list(reg = reg, pred = reg + sum(w * (y - X %*% beta)), w = w, d0 = d0)
}
new_site <- krige(30, 20, 2450)
top3 <- order(-abs(new_site$w))[1:3]
resid_sp <- as.vector(y - X %*% beta)

snow$pos <- numFactor(snow$x_km, snow$y_km)
snow$all <- factor(1)
fit_tmb <- glmmTMB(swe_cm ~ elev_km + exp(pos + 0 | all), data = snow)

r_lm <- resid(fit_lm)
```

**NRES 746, Week 14, Lecture 1: Neighbors (take-home)**

\ans{\textbf{Answer key.} Answers are in magenta sans-serif type; longer answers have a bar in the margin.}

**Due Tuesday, Dec. 1.** Work on your own or in small groups. Parts 1
and 2 are on paper; Part 3 and the optional Part 4 involve R. Turn in
this sheet only: you'll make a figure and write code along the way,
but no need to submit them.

A water district forecasts its spring supply from snow courses:
permanent sites where surveyors sample the snowpack by hand. It has
April 1 snow water equivalent (SWE, the depth of water in the snowpack,
in cm) from 60 snow courses spread over a 60 by 40 km mountain range.
It wants to know how fast SWE rises with elevation, and how much snow
to expect at a site where it has proposed adding a station. Storms
don't deliver snow evenly, so stations near each other tend to be alike in ways elevation doesn't fully explain.

## Notation and key equations

- $y_i$: SWE at station $i$ (cm). $e_i$: its residual from a
  regression of SWE on elevation.
- $\text{Var}(y)$ is a variance, $\text{Cov}(y_1, y_2)$ a covariance.
  If $y_1$ and $y_2$ each have variance $\sigma^2$ and correlation
  $\rho$, then $\text{Cov}(y_1, y_2) = \rho\sigma^2$. For constants $a$
  and $b$, $\text{Var}(a y_1 + b y_2) = a^2\text{Var}(y_1) +
  b^2\text{Var}(y_2) + 2ab\,\text{Cov}(y_1, y_2)$.
- $d$ or $d_{ij}$: distance between two locations (km).
- **Semivariance** $\gamma(d)$: half the expected squared difference
  between the residuals at two locations $d$ km apart,
  $\gamma(d) = \tfrac{1}{2}E\big[(e_i - e_j)^2\big]$ for $d_{ij} = d$.
  A **variogram** plots semivariance against $d$; the points in an empirical
  variogram average $\tfrac{1}{2}(e_i - e_j)^2$ over all pairs of
  stations in each distance bin. Similar neighbors make $\gamma(d)$
  small at short distances.
- On a variogram, the **nugget** is the height the curve starts from
  just above $d = 0$, the **sill** is the level where it flattens out,
  and the **range** is the distance where it (nearly) reaches the sill,
  beyond which residuals are effectively uncorrelated.
- $\sigma_s$: SD of the spatially smooth part of the residuals;
  $\sigma_e$: SD of the independent station-level noise; $\ell$:
  length-scale (km), how quickly the smooth part's correlation fades
  with distance; $\rho(d)$: correlation of the smooth part at two
  locations $d$ km apart.
- $\mathbf{y} \sim \text{MVN}(\boldsymbol\mu, V)$: the multivariate
  normal, with mean vector $\boldsymbol\mu$ and covariance matrix $V$
  ($V_{ii}$ is station $i$'s variance, $V_{ij}$ the covariance of
  stations $i$ and $j$). $X$ is the model matrix and
  $\boldsymbol\beta$ the coefficients ($\beta_0$ the intercept,
  $\beta_1$ the elevation slope), so $\boldsymbol\mu =
  X\boldsymbol\beta$.

## Part 1: Two stations (on paper)

Two stations have SWE values $y_1$ and $y_2$. Each has variance
$\sigma^2$, and their correlation is $\rho$.

**1a.** Find the variance of their mean, $\bar y = (y_1 + y_2)/2$, in
terms of $\sigma^2$ and $\rho$.

\ansbegin

$$\text{Var}(\bar y) = \tfrac{1}{4}\left[\text{Var}(y_1) + \text{Var}(y_2) + 2\,\text{Cov}(y_1, y_2)\right]
= \tfrac{1}{4}\left[2\sigma^2 + 2\rho\sigma^2\right] = \frac{\sigma^2 (1 + \rho)}{2}$$

\ansend

**1b.** Fill in the table. $n$ independent stations have
$\text{Var}(\bar y) = \sigma^2 / n$; the last column asks what $n$
would give the same variance as these two correlated stations.

```{r rho-table, fig.height=1.85}
rho <- c(0, 0.5, 0.9)
blank_table(
  headers = list(expression(rho), expression(Var(bar(y)) / sigma^2), "equivalent number of independent stations"),
  body = lapply(rho, function(r) list(format(r), sprintf("%.2f", (1 + r) / 2), sprintf("%.2f", 2 / (1 + r)))),
  col_widths = c(0.7, 1.6, 2.7), fill_cols = 2:3)
```

## Part 2: Reading a variogram (on paper)

A regression of SWE on elevation leaves residuals. The figure shows
their semivariance against the distance between stations, in 5-km
bins.

```{r variogram, fig.width=6.2, fig.height=3.6}
library(gstat)
library(sp)
snow_sp <- snow[, c("x_km", "y_km")]
snow_sp$r <- r_lm
coordinates(snow_sp) <- ~ x_km + y_km
vg <- variogram(r ~ 1, snow_sp, cutoff = 30, width = 5)
par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(vg$dist, vg$gamma, type = "n", xlim = c(0, 30), ylim = c(0, 150), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i",
     xlab = "Distance between stations (km)", ylab = expression("Semivariance of residuals (" * cm^2 * ")"))
abline(v = seq(0, 30, 5), h = seq(0, 150, 25), col = "grey88")
points(vg$dist, vg$gamma, pch = 19, cex = 1.2)
curve(sigma_e^2 + sigma_s^2 * (1 - exp(-x / ell)), add = TRUE, col = ans_col, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("bottomright", "fitted spatial model (Part 3)", col = ans_col, lwd = 2, lty = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.85,
       text.col = ans_col, text.font = 3)
box()
```

**2a.** Sketch a smooth variogram curve through the points, and read
off rough values:

nugget \ans{about 10 to 30} $\qquad$ sill \ans{about 100 to 120} $\qquad$ range \ans{about 15 to 25} km

\ansbegin

Any smooth rising curve that levels off is fine.

\ansend

**2b.** The semivariance drops at the largest distances. Is there any
reason to think semivariance could decrease with distance, and is that
realistic for this system?

\ansbegin

A drop means stations far apart are more alike than stations at middle
distances, which takes a repeating pattern (a "hole effect"), such as
ridges and valleys at a regular spacing. Storm-driven snow over a
60 by 40 km range has no reason to repeat every 20 km or so, so the
drop is noise: with patches about 20 km across, the range holds only a
few independent patches. The far bins have plenty of pairs
(`r vg$np[nrow(vg)]` in the last one), but those pairs all share the
same few patches. Don't bend the curve down to follow them.

\ansend

**2c.** The correlation between the residuals of two stations $d$ km
apart is $1 - \gamma(d)/\text{sill}$. From your curve, about what is
the correlation for stations 5 km apart?

\ansbegin

Reading $\gamma(5) \approx 40$ and a sill of about 110:
$1 - 40/110 \approx 0.6$. Anything from 0.5 to 0.7 is
reasonable. (The fitted model in Part 3 gives
`r sprintf("%.2f", sigma_s^2 * exp(-5 / ell) / (sigma_s^2 + sigma_e^2))`.)

\ansend

## Part 3: The spatial model, by hand

Each coding question has a label:

- *Recommended: no AI*: this week's core skill. R's help pages, web
  search, the Week 14 page, and classmates are fine.
- *AI optional/encouraged*: the results matter, but the code isn't the
  point.

Read the data with

```{r read-data, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
snow <- read.csv(
  "https://kevintshoemaker.github.io/NRES-746/data/SnowCourses.csv")
snow$elev_km <- (snow$elev_m - 2400) / 1000      # km above 2400 m
```

The columns are the station, its easting and northing in km (`x_km`,
`y_km`), elevation (`elev_m`), and April 1 SWE (`swe_cm`).

**3a.** *(AI optional/encouraged.)* Fit `lm(swe_cm ~ elev_km, data = snow)`
and make a map of the stations with the symbol size or color showing
each residual (for yourself; don't turn it in).

SWE rises \ans{`r sprintf("%.1f", coef(fit_lm)[2])`} cm per km of elevation (SE \ans{`r sprintf("%.1f", summary(fit_lm)$coefficients[2, 2])`})

```{r fig-3a, fig.width=6, fig.height=4.2}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1.5, 1))
plot(snow$x_km, snow$y_km, asp = 1, pch = ifelse(r_lm > 0, 16, 1), cex = 0.5 + abs(r_lm) / 6, col = ans_col,
     xlab = "Easting (km)", ylab = "Northing (km)", main = "Sample residual map", cex.main = 0.9, col.main = ans_col)
points(30, 20, pch = 4, cex = 1.5, lwd = 2)
legend("topright", c("above the line", "below the line", "new site (Part 4)"), pch = c(16, 1, 4),
       col = c(ans_col, ans_col, "black"), bg = "white", cex = 0.75, title = "size = |residual|")
```

Describe the map: are residuals of the same sign scattered or grouped,
and where are the largest positive and negative ones?

\ansbegin

Grouped: neighboring stations tend to share a sign. Stations east of
40 km mostly sit below the line (mean residual
`r sprintf("%.1f", mean(r_lm[snow$x_km > 40]))` cm); the largest
positive residuals are in the west and center (S28, S51, S04), and the
largest negative ones in the far northwest and the east (S18, S23,
S12).

\ansend

The spatial model is

$$\mathbf{y} \sim \text{MVN}(X\boldsymbol\beta,\ V), \qquad
V_{ij} = \sigma_s^2 \exp(-d_{ij}/\ell) + \sigma_e^2\,[i = j]$$

where $d_{ij}$ is the distance in km between stations $i$ and $j$, and
$[i = j]$ is 1 on the diagonal and 0 elsewhere.

**3b.** *(Recommended: no AI.)* Write a function `nll_spatial(par)` that
returns the negative log-likelihood, where `par` holds the intercept,
the elevation slope, $\log\sigma_s$, $\log\ell$, and $\log\sigma_e$, in
that order. Check it: `nll_spatial(c(40, 40, log(8), log(10), log(3)))`
should return `r sprintf("%.2f", check_val)`.

Your value: \ans{`r sprintf("%.2f", check_val)`}

As $\ell$ shrinks toward 0, what happens to the off-diagonal entries of
the covariance matrix $V$, and what familiar model is left?

\ansbegin

They go to 0 (each is $\sigma_s^2 \exp(-d_{ij}/\ell)$ with
$d_{ij} > 0$), so
$V = (\sigma_s^2 + \sigma_e^2) I$: independent errors with one
variance, the ordinary regression.

\ansend

**3c.** *(Recommended: no AI.)* Minimize it with `optim()`
(`method = "BFGS"`, `hessian = TRUE`), starting from the values in the
check above. Confirm `$convergence` is 0, and fill in the table.

```{r fit-table, fig.height=1.6, dev=if (knitr::is_latex_output()) "cairo_pdf" else "png"}
blank_table(
  headers = expression("", atop("slope", hat(beta)[1]), atop("SE of slope", SE(hat(beta)[1])),
                       atop("spatial SD", hat(sigma)[s]), atop("length-scale", hat("ℓ") ~ "(km)"),
                       atop("noise SD", hat(sigma)[e]), "logLik"),
  header_height = 0.6,
  body = list(list("lm()", sprintf("%.1f", coef(fit_lm)[2]), sprintf("%.1f", summary(fit_lm)$coefficients[2, 2]),
                   "(none)", "(none)", sprintf("%.1f", sigma(fit_lm)), sprintf("%.1f", logLik(fit_lm))),
              list("spatial", sprintf("%.1f", beta[2]), sprintf("%.1f", se[2]), sprintf("%.1f", sigma_s),
                   sprintf("%.1f", ell), sprintf("%.1f", sigma_e), sprintf("%.1f", -fit$value))),
  col_widths = c(1, 1, 1.2, 1, 1, 1, 1.1), fill_cols = 2:7)
```

\ansbegin

`sigma(fit_lm)` is `r sprintf("%.1f", sigma(fit_lm))`; the maximum
likelihood value, `r sprintf("%.1f", sqrt(mean(r_lm^2)))`, is also
fine.

\ansend

**3d.** How do $\hat\sigma_e^2$, $\hat\sigma_s^2 + \hat\sigma_e^2$, and
$2\hat\ell$ compare with the nugget, sill, and range you estimated visually in 2a?

\ansbegin

$\hat\sigma_e^2 =$ `r sprintf("%.0f", sigma_e^2)` (nugget),
$\hat\sigma_s^2 + \hat\sigma_e^2 =$ `r sprintf("%.0f", sigma_s^2 + sigma_e^2)`
(sill), $2\hat\ell =$ `r sprintf("%.0f", 2 * ell)` km (range): in line
with the variogram, with a nugget at the low end of what the points
suggest.

\ansend

**3e.** Final question: where did you use AI, if anywhere, and what did you have to
check or fix? If you didn't use it, what was hardest to get working?

\ansbegin

Open-ended.

\ansend

## Part 4, Bonus (optional): Predicting at a new site

The district is considering a new station at easting 30 km, northing
20 km, elevation 2450 m.

From the spatial model's intercept and slope alone (SWE as a function
of elevation), the predicted SWE at the new site is
`r sprintf("%.1f", new_site$reg)` cm.

The model can do better, because nearby stations say something about
the unmeasured part of the snowpack there. Let $\mathbf{k}_0$ hold the
covariance between the field at the new site and at each station,
$k_{0i} = \hat\sigma_s^2 \exp(-d_{0i}/\hat\ell)$, with $d_{0i}$ the
distance from the new site to station $i$. The prediction is

$$\hat y_0 = \mathbf{x}_0^T\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} +
\mathbf{k}_0^T\, V^{-1} (\mathbf{y} - X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})$$

**4a.** *(Recommended: no AI.)* Compute $\hat y_0$ in R (`solve(V, b)`
gives $V^{-1}\mathbf{b}$).

$\hat y_0 =$ \ans{`r sprintf("%.1f", new_site$pred)`} cm

**4b.** The entries of $\mathbf{k}_0^T V^{-1}$ are the weights each
station's residual gets. Which three stations have the largest weights,
and how far is each from the new site? Why did the prediction move the
way it did from the elevation-only prediction?

\ansbegin

`r paste0(snow$station[top3], " (", sprintf("%.1f", new_site$d0[top3]), " km, weight ", sprintf("%.2f", new_site$w[top3]), ", residual ", sprintf("%+.1f", resid_sp[top3]), " cm)", collapse = "; ")`.
The nearest stations get the most weight, and they hold more snow than
their elevations predict, so the prediction rises by
`r sprintf("%.1f", new_site$pred - new_site$reg)` cm.

\ansend

**4c.** Fit the same model with `glmmTMB` and compare log-likelihoods:

```{r glmmtmb-syntax, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
library(glmmTMB)
snow$pos <- numFactor(snow$x_km, snow$y_km)   # station coordinates
snow$all <- factor(1)                         # one field over all stations
fit_tmb <- glmmTMB(swe_cm ~ elev_km + exp(pos + 0 | all), data = snow)
logLik(fit_tmb)
```

Yours: \ans{`r sprintf("%.2f", -fit$value)`} $\qquad$ `glmmTMB`: \ans{`r sprintf("%.2f", logLik(fit_tmb))`}
